questions.question: Select the option that expresses the following sentence in the superlative degree of comparison. She is talented among her peers.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in the superlative degree of comparison.

She is talented among her peers.

options.text: She is the most talented among her peers.
options.html: She is the most talented among her peers.

options.text: She is talented compared to her peers.
options.html: She is talented compared to her peers.

options.text: She is more talented than her peers.
options.html: She is more talented than her peers.

options.text: She is as talented as her peers.
options.html: She is as talented as her peers.

questions.solution:
Option (a) uses the superlative degree ("the most talented") to imply that she is the most talented person in the group of peers. This is a stronger statement, saying she stands out as the best, which fits well with the idea of being the most talented in comparison to all others.

The given sentence and options b) and d) are in the positive degrees, while option c) is in the comparative degree.

Hence, option (a) is correct.

Note:

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

questions.solution:
The original sentence, "This is the largest tree in the park," is in the superlative degree of comparison. To transform it into a positive degree, we must ensure the sentence uses "as...as" to indicate comparison without implying comparative or superlative status.

Option a) is correct. It uses the positive degree ("as large as") and compares this tree to other trees in the park without explicitly stating it is the largest.

Options b) and c) are in the superlative degrees, while option d) is in the comparative degree.

Hence, option (a) is correct.

Note:

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

questions.solution:
The past perfect tense is used to talk about an action that happened before another action in the past. In this sentence, the action "had lived in the city" occurred before the action "moved to the countryside".

Option (a)- This uses the past continuous tense, which is incorrect in this context.

Option (b)- This uses the simple past tense, which is incorrect in this context.

Option (c) - This uses the past perfect tense in partially correct form, as the verb "live" should be in the past participle form "lived" instead of the -ing form "living", and the form should be "had lived" instead of "had living".

Hence, the correct answer is option (d).

Note:

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

questions.solution:
The correct option is a).

This sentence correctly uses the future perfect continuous tense (will have been + present participle). This tense is ideal here because it focuses on the duration ("for exactly two years") of an activity (saving money) that will continue up to a specific point in the future ("In March").

· Option (b): This uses an incorrect passive construction ("will be saved"). "My brother" (the subject) is the one performing the action ("saving money"), so the active voice is needed.

· Option (c): This is grammatically incorrect. The structure "will have" should be followed by a past participle, but here it is followed by a present participle ("saving") without the necessary "been."

· Option (d): This is grammatically incorrect. "will have" must be followed by a past participle, not the base form of the verb ("save").

Note: Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

· Option (a): This uses the present continuous tense ("is converting"), which is for actions happening right now or temporary situations. A scientific fact is permanent, not temporary.

· Option (a): This has a subject-verb agreement error. The singular subject "scientist" requires the singular verb "was," not the plural "were."

· Option (c): This uses the past perfect continuous tense, which is for actions that were ongoing before another past action. It is not suitable for a single, completed event like this.

· Option (d): This incorrectly uses the present perfect tense ("have accepted"). This tense is for actions with a present connection, not for actions at a specified finished time like "last month." Also, the plural "have" is incorrect for the singular subject "scientist".

Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).
